candidates.title: Meteor Tally Night
candidates.pitch: The visitor lies back in a procedural night sky and counts meteors the way real visual observers do: tap or press Space for each streak, or plot its start and end so the page can check whether the trail points back to the shower's radiant. The sky is driven by a real rate model (radiant altitude, moonlight, light pollution, trees blocking the view), so the choice of observing spot matters: an apple orchard hides part of the sky, a bare granite ridge shows all of it. At dawn a thermal-paper observing receipt prints with the visitor's count, the estimated true zenithal rate, and how many faint ones slipped by.
candidates.whyNow: The Orionids peak on the night of Oct 21-22, 2026 under a bright waxing gibbous moon, while today (Oct 10) is a new moon with dark skies, so the page can show the moon-versus-meteor tradeoff both ways. It keeps working for any date because the moon and radiant are computed.

research.summary: Several independent guides agree the 2026 Orionids peak on the night of Oct 21-22 with the full moon on Oct 26, so the moon is roughly 77-80% lit and sets around 3 a.m., leaving a dark window before dawn. The shower comes from debris of Halley's comet, radiates from a point north of Betelgeuse in Orion, and arrives at roughly 66 km/s with a zenithal rate near 20 per hour. The standard observer correction chain (radiant altitude via sin(h), limiting magnitude via population index to the power 6.5 minus LM, obstructed-field factor) is documented in encyclopedic and paper sources, and Bortle classes map to naked-eye limiting magnitudes. Those real formulas become the game engine: the sky is a model the player learns to read, not random decoration. A population index near 2.5 appeared in only one result, so it is an assumed constant, labelled as such.

facts.claim: The 2026 Orionids are predicted to peak on the night of Oct 21-22, with the maximum around 18 UTC on Oct 21 (per the RASC handbook as cited by EarthSky).
On the Orionid peak nights of 2026 the moon is a waxing gibbous roughly 77-80% lit and sets around 3 a.m. local time, leaving a dark window before dawn.
New moon is on 2026-10-10 at 15:50 UTC and the full Hunter's Moon on 2026-10-26 at about 04:12 UTC.
The Orionid zenithal hourly rate is about 20 per hour (reported as 20 to about 23 depending on source), from debris of comet 1P/Halley.
The Orionid radiant lies just north of Betelgeuse in Orion and the meteors enter at roughly 66 km/s.
Visual rates are corrected to a ZHR with the factor r^(6.5 - LM) for limiting magnitude, a divide by sin of radiant altitude, and 1/(1-k) for an obstructed fraction k of the field.
Bortle sky classes map to naked-eye limiting magnitudes, for example class 4 about 6.1-6.5, class 7 about 5.0, class 9 about 4.0 or less; the values depend on the observer.

inspirations: visual meteor counting sessions run by amateur astronomy groups

design.coreLoop: A compressed night (about one real minute per sky hour) plays out under a procedural sky. Meteors arrive as a Poisson stream whose rate follows the shower's ZHR, the radiant's altitude, the sky's limiting magnitude and the fraction of sky blocked by the chosen spot; each meteor has a brightness drawn from a population-index distribution, so the faint ones are genuinely hard to catch. The visitor counts by tapping or pressing Space, and in plot mode marks start and end so trails that point back to the radiant are scored as shower members and the rest as sporadics. The night ends with a receipt that compares the visitor's tally against the hidden truth log and back-computes an estimated ZHR. Repeating with a different spot, date or moon teaches why the numbers move; the tenth night is about technique: scanning away from the moon, resting the eyes, and plotting accurately.
sophisticationHooks: Real rate engine: ZHR times sin(radiant altitude) times r^(LM-6.5) times the unobstructed fraction, plus a sporadic background, with radiant altitude computed from latitude, date and time
Moon module (phase, altitude and a moonlight term in the limiting magnitude) self-checked against the sourced new moon of 2026-10-10 15:50 UTC and full moon of 2026-10-26 about 04:12 UTC
Plot-and-classify skill layer: backward-extended trails that hit the radiant box score as shower meteors, with an accuracy grade

Observing spots as terrain silhouettes (orchard rows, granite ridge, rooftop, field) with different obstruction and light-dome values, plus a procedural thermal receipt (WebAudio printer chirps, tear-off animation) and a URL hash that carries seed, date, spot and result for a friend to compare
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: canvas sky with a hand-made bright-star set (about 150 stars plus Orion), Orionids model with real parameters, 2 to 3 further showers marked as approximate hand-made data, moon routine, 4 observing spots, count and plot modes, receipt renderer, light/dark (day-sky red-light mode vs paper mode), reduced-motion static replay, keyboard and touch, about panel, hash state. Cut: geolocation, live weather, planets, satellite passes, accounts, leaderboards.
risks: Only the Orionid parameters are verified; any other shower's dates and rates are hand-made approximations and must be labelled as such on the page, or cut.
The population index near 2.5 was seen in one result only (unverified); the page labels it an assumed constant.
Sunrise, moon position and radiant altitude come from low-precision hand-coded formulas: show them as approximate and keep the moon self-check against the sourced phase times as a test.
Counting meteors can feel passive; the plot-and-classify mode, spot choice and receipt feedback must land in the first two minutes or the loop is thin.
Not a forecast or observing advice: the page is a simulation with simulated meteors, labelled as such, and the real Orionid facts are shown as 'as of 2026-10-10, per' the listed sources.

candidates.title: Backyard Rink Keeper
candidates.pitch: The visitor tends a backyard hockey rink through one invented winter: reading a five-day forecast fan, choosing when to lay the liner, flood thin layers or one deep pour, scrape and resurface, and when to lace up. A cut-away canvas shows the ice growing in banded layers, trapped air, a thaw crack, snow insulating the surface, and ground frost as hard as granite beneath the liner. The season ends with a receipt of skating nights, puck-drop evenings and ice sins, and the seed in the URL lets a friend replay the same winter and compare.
candidates.whyNow: Hockey season opened on Sept 29, 2026, the first outdoor game of the year is the Oct 25 Heritage Classic, and backyard rink builders start prepping before the first hard freeze. It still works in any month because every winter is seeded.

research.summary: Ice thickness under cold air grows roughly with the square root of accumulated freezing degree-days (Stefan's relation), which gives the sim a real engine: early cold nights add ice fast, later ones slowly, and a thaw stalls or reverses growth. Backyard rink guides give practical targets such as about 4 inches (10 cm) finished and more for adults, wait for several consecutive days below about -4 C before the first flood, and test the surface before skating; they disagree on whether to flood in thin layers or in one pour, which becomes a strategy choice in the game. The hockey calendar supplies the hook: the NHL season opened Sept 29, 2026 and an outdoor Heritage Classic game is set for Oct 25. Practical rink guidance is reported by single sources and is shown as reported, not confirmed.

facts.claim: Ice thickness grows approximately in proportion to the square root of accumulated freezing degree-days (Stefan's relation); thaws stall or reverse growth.
An outdoor Heritage Classic game between two Canadian clubs is scheduled for Sunday 2026-10-25 in Winnipeg.

As of 2026-10-10, per the Canadian Tire kit guide, a finished backyard rink should have at least about 4 inches (10 cm) of ice, with about 6 inches suggested for adults (reported by one source, unconfirmed).
As of 2026-10-10, per the Innisfil municipal guide, the first flood is best delayed until several consecutive cold days, reported as 7 to 10 days at or below -10 C (single source, unconfirmed).

As of 2026-10-10, rink guides reportedly disagree on flooding in thin layers (Sunapee page) versus a single deep pour on a liner (other retail guides); neither school is confirmed by two independent sources.

design.coreLoop: Each in-game day the visitor reads a temperature forecast drawn as a widening fan, then chooses an action: set the liner, flood a thin layer, make a deep pour, shovel snow, scrape and hot-water resurface, or skate. A Stefan-style growth engine turns each night's freezing degree-days into new ice for the water that was laid down, while warm spells, snow insulation, wind and overuse add flaws such as bumps, air gaps and cracks that show in the cut-away. Skating on good ice earns the points that matter and wears the surface; skating on thin or bumpy ice costs ice quality. The choice between thin layers and a single pour has a real tradeoff, and forecast uncertainty makes each night a small gamble. The second and tenth winters differ because seeds change the cold snaps, the January thaw and the snow timing.
sophisticationHooks: Physics-flavoured engine: square-root freezing-degree-day growth per layer with a re-flood starting-thickness term, snow-cover insulation, thaw stall, and a toy coefficient derived from standard ice constants then tuned for feel
Seeded synthetic winters (autocorrelated temperature, cold snaps, a mid-season thaw, snow events) with a forecast-fan whose error grows with lead time, so planning under uncertainty is the core skill
Cut-away canvas of ground frost, liner, banded ice layers and bubbles, plus a yard view with boards, light and puck-scuff trails drawn procedurally
Season receipt with grades and a URL hash (seed, difficulty, final score) for replaying the same winter against a friend; procedural audio for scrape, pour and skate
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: seeded weather generator, ice growth and quality model, forecast fan chart, action bar with keyboard shortcuts and touch buttons, cut-away and yard canvases, 3 difficulty presets, season receipt, hash state, about panel with the sourced facts shown as dated, light/dark, reduced-motion static redraw. Cut: real weather data, geolocation, multi-yard maps, multiplayer, any real team art.
risks: Practical rink advice (4 inch target, 7 to 10 cold days, thin layers versus one pour) is single-source and unverified; the page shows these as 'as of 2026-10-10, per <guide>' or leaves them out, and the sim's thresholds are labelled game settings.
Ice-thickness coefficient is tuned for play, not measured; the page states clearly that this is a toy and must never be used to judge whether real ice is safe.
Winters are invented and seeded, never a forecast of any real place; label every temperature as simulated.
Management sims can turn into spreadsheet clicking; the cut-away visuals, forecast gamble and receipt voice must carry delight in the first two minutes.
Team and venue names appear only as dated references in the about panel and no logos or art are used.
